to-string.title: How serde_json::to_string() works
to-string.description: Turns a value into a compact JSON string; struct fields become keys.

slides.caption: #[derive(Serialize)] lets serde walk the struct field by field. to_string() writes each part as JSON text.
A struct becomes a JSON object, so the output starts with {.
The field name becomes the key "name". Its value is a String, so it is written in quotes: "Ann".
A comma separates the entries. The field age becomes "age"; 30 is a number, so it has no quotes.
The object is closed with }. to_string() adds no spaces or line breaks.
to_string(&user) returns Ok with {"name":"Ann","age":30}. The keys are in the order the fields are declared.

to-string-pretty.title: How serde_json::to_string_pretty() works
to-string-pretty.description: Same JSON as to_string(), laid out on several lines for people to read.

slides.caption: to_string_pretty() writes the same data as to_string(), but with line breaks, 2-space indentation and a space after each colon.
The object opens on its own line.
Each entry gets its own line, indented by 2 spaces: "name": "Ann", followed by a comma.
The last entry has no comma after it.
The closing } goes on its own line, back at the left edge.
Compact: {"name":"Ann","age":30}. Pretty: the four lines shown. A parser reads both as the same value.

from-str.title: How serde_json::from_str() works
from-str.description: Parses JSON text into a typed value; a missing field is an error.

note.text: #[derive(Deserialize)] struct User { name: String, age: u32 }

l4.text: no "age" key, and age is not an Option

slides.caption: from_str() reads JSON text and fills in the struct. The type, User, says which keys are needed and what type each value must have.
Each key is matched to the field with the same name, and each value is checked: "Ann" is a string, 30 fits in a u32.
All fields were found, so the result is Ok(User).
Now the JSON has no "age" key.
age has no default and is not an Option, so the value cannot be built.
from_str() returns an Err that names the missing field and the position where the object ended.
Make a field Option<u32> or add #[serde(default)] when it may be missing. Unknown extra keys are ignored by default.

to-value.title: How serde_json::to_value() works
to-value.description: Turns a value into a serde_json::Value, the general JSON tree.

slides.caption: to_value() builds a tree in memory instead of text. Every JSON thing has a Value variant: Null, Bool, Number, String, Array, Object.
The struct becomes Value::Object, a map from String keys to Values.
Each field becomes an entry: "Ann" → Value::String("Ann") and 30 → Value::Number(30).
The map is a BTreeMap by default, so the keys are sorted: "age" comes before "name". Enable the preserve_order feature to keep the field order.
You can now read and change the tree, e.g. v["age"] = json!(31), and turn it back into a struct with from_value().

from-value.title: How serde_json::from_value() works
from-value.description: Turns a serde_json::Value tree into a typed struct.

slides.caption: from_value() is from_str() for a Value that is already parsed. It takes the Value by value (it is moved, not borrowed).
The entry "name" fills the field name; String("Ann") becomes the Rust String "Ann".
The entry "age" fills age; Number(30) must fit in a u32, which it does.
Every field is filled, so the result is Ok(User). A Number(-1) or String("30") for age would be an Err instead.
from_value(v) gives Ok(User { name: "Ann", age: 30 }). Pass v.clone() if you still need the Value afterwards.

value-get.title: How Value::get() works
value-get.description: Looks up a key (or an index) and returns None when it is not there.

slides.caption: get() takes a key for objects or an index for arrays. It returns Option<&Value>, so a missing key is not a panic.
v.get("name"): the key exists, so it returns Some(&String("Ann")).
v.get("zip"): no entry has that key, so it returns None.
v["zip"] would also not panic: indexing a Value returns Value::Null for a missing key. get() makes the difference visible.
Chain with and_then: v.get("name").and_then(|n| n.as_str()) gives Some("Ann").

value-pointer.title: How Value::pointer() works
value-pointer.description: Follows a path like "/user/tags/0" into nested JSON.

slides.caption: pointer() takes a JSON Pointer: path segments separated by /. Each segment is an object key or an array index.
"user" is a key of the top object: step into its value.
"tags" is a key of that object: its value is an array.
In an array, the segment is an index: 0 is the first item, "admin".
pointer("/user/tags/0") is Some("admin"). If any step is missing, for example "/user/tags/5", the result is None.

value-as-i64.title: How Value::as_i64() works
value-as-i64.description: Reads a JSON number as i64; anything else gives None.

note.text: a JSON string is not a number

slides.caption: as_i64() returns Some(n) only when the Value is a number that fits in an i64.
Number(30) is a whole number that fits: Some(30).
String("30") holds text. as_i64() does not convert text, so it gives None.
Number(30.5) would also give None: it is not a whole number. Use as_f64() for it, or parse the string yourself.
JSON from other programs often has numbers in quotes. as_str() and then .parse::<i64>() reads those.

value-as-str.title: How Value::as_str works
value-as-str.description: The text of a JSON string, or None for any other kind of value.

slides.caption: JSON values come in six kinds. as_str() answers only for strings, and borrows the text without copying it.
42 is a number, not text: None. It does not convert numbers to text.
Use v.to_string() to get any value as JSON text instead.

value-as-u64.title: How Value::as_u64 works
value-as-u64.description: A JSON number as u64, if it is a whole number that fits.

slides.caption: as_u64() succeeds only for numbers that are whole and not negative.
-1 is negative: None (as_i64 would give Some(-1)).
2.5 has a fraction: None. Floats are never rounded.
as_i64 for signed numbers, as_f64 for any number.

value-as-f64.title: How Value::as_f64 works
value-as-f64.description: Any JSON number as f64; None for other kinds.

slides.caption: Every JSON number can be read as a float, whole numbers included.
"4" is a string: None. Text is not parsed.
Very large integers may lose precision as f64.

value-as-bool.title: How Value::as_bool works
value-as-bool.description: The value of a JSON true/false, or None.

slides.caption: The text "true" is a string, not a boolean.

value-as-array.title: How Value::as_array works
value-as-array.description: Borrows a JSON array as &Vec<Value>, or None.

slides.caption: as_array() gives you the Vec inside a JSON array, so you can loop over it.
[1, 2, 3] is an array: Some, with 3 items.
An object is not an array: None.
v.as_array().map(|a| a.len()) gives the lengths shown here.

value-as-object.title: How Value::as_object works
value-as-object.description: Borrows a JSON object as &Map<String, Value>, or None.

slides.caption: The Map keeps the keys; use it to list or check them.

value-as-array-mut.title: How Value::as_array_mut works
value-as-array-mut.description: A mutable &mut Vec<Value> inside a JSON array.

slides.caption: None if the value is not an array.

value-as-object-mut.title: How Value::as_object_mut works
value-as-object-mut.description: A mutable &mut Map inside a JSON object.

slides.caption: None if it is not an object.
Missing keys give None from get(), not null.

value-as-null.title: How Value::as_null works
value-as-null.description: Some(()) for JSON null, None otherwise.

slides.caption: Handy with the ? operator in Option chains.
Numbers are not strings, even "1" vs 1.

value-is-number.title: How Value::is_number works
value-is-number.description: true for any JSON number, whole or not.

slides.caption: A number written in quotes is a string.

value-is-boolean.title: How Value::is_boolean works
value-is-boolean.description: true for JSON true and false.

value-is-i64.title: How Value::is_i64 works
value-is-i64.description: true if the number is a whole number that fits in i64.

slides.caption: 2.0 is stored as a float, so it is not an i64.
is_u64 and is_f64 check the other storage kinds.

value-is-u64.title: How Value::is_u64 works
value-is-u64.description: true if the number is a whole number ≥ 0 that fits in u64.

value-is-f64.title: How Value::is_f64 works
value-is-f64.description: true if the number was written with a fraction or exponent.

slides.caption: How the number was written decides how it is stored.

value-get-mut.title: How Value::get_mut works
value-get-mut.description: A mutable reference to a field or array item, if it exists.

note.text: None when the key is missing

slides.caption: get_mut takes a key for objects or an index for arrays and lets you replace that value in place.
"n" exists, so get_mut gives Some(&mut Value).
Assign a new value through it.
v.get_mut("missing") is None: it never adds keys.

value-pointer-mut.title: How Value::pointer_mut works
value-pointer-mut.description: A mutable reference to a nested value, found by a JSON Pointer like "/a/0".

slides.caption: Each /part is an object key or an array index.

value-take.title: How Value::take works
value-take.description: Moves the value out and leaves null in its place.

slides.caption: take() is like std::mem::take: you get the value, and Null stays behind.
The key is still there, but now holds null.
Useful to move big values out of a document without copying.

from-slice.title: How serde_json::from_slice works
from-slice.description: Parses JSON from bytes into any type that implements Deserialize.

slides.caption: from_slice is from_str for &[u8]: handy for data read from files or the network.
The bytes are parsed as JSON.
The fields fill a User (derive Deserialize).
Invalid UTF-8 or JSON gives an Err with line and column.

from-reader.title: How serde_json::from_reader works
from-reader.description: Parses JSON from anything that implements io::Read, such as a File.

slides.caption: Wrap files in BufReader: from_reader reads byte by byte.
from_str is faster when the text is already in memory.

to-vec.title: How serde_json::to_vec works
to-vec.description: Serializes a value as compact JSON bytes.

slides.caption: Same text as to_string, as a Vec<u8>.
Ready to write to a socket or file.

to-vec-pretty.title: How serde_json::to_vec_pretty works
to-vec-pretty.description: Serializes a value as indented JSON bytes.

slides.caption: Two-space indent, one item per line.

to-writer.title: How serde_json::to_writer works
to-writer.description: Serializes a value straight into an io::Write, such as a File.

slides.caption: No String is built in between.

to-writer-pretty.title: How serde_json::to_writer_pretty works
to-writer-pretty.description: Writes indented JSON into an io::Write.

slides.caption: Good for config files people edit.

stream-into-iter.title: How Deserializer::into_iter works
stream-into-iter.description: Reads many JSON values one after another from one input.

slides.caption: A StreamDeserializer yields one Result<Value> per JSON value found, separated by whitespace.

deserializer-from-str.title: How Deserializer::from_str works
deserializer-from-str.description: Creates a JSON deserializer over a &str, for streaming or custom use.

slides.caption: Then call into_iter, or pass it to Deserialize::deserialize.
serde_json::from_str handles the common single-value case.
Insert keys, then wrap with Value::Object(map).

map-insert.title: How Map::insert works
map-insert.description: Sets a key, returning the old value if there was one.

slides.caption: Keys are Strings; values are Values. Inserting an existing key replaces its value.
"a" already exists: the old value 1 comes back.

map-get.title: How Map::get works
map-get.description: Looks up a key in a JSON object map.

slides.caption: A key holding null still exists.

map-remove.title: How Map::remove works
map-remove.description: Removes a key and returns its value.

slides.caption: None if the key was missing.
With preserve_order, prefer shift_remove to keep the order.
Sorted by key unless the preserve_order feature is on.
values() and iter() give the rest.
&m in a for loop does the same.
Nested objects count as one value.

map-is-empty.title: How Map::is_empty works
map-is-empty.description: true if the map has no keys.

slides.caption: Use it to skip empty objects.

map-entry.title: How Map::entry works
map-entry.description: The entry for a key, to insert or update in one lookup.

slides.caption: entry() finds the slot for a key; or_insert fills it only if it was empty.
"hits" is missing: the entry is Vacant.
and_modify changes an existing value instead.

entry-or-insert.title: How Entry::or_insert works (serde_json)
entry-or-insert.description: Returns the value for the key, inserting a default first if missing.

slides.caption: The returned &mut Value lets you update it.

entry-or-insert-with.title: How Entry::or_insert_with works (serde_json)
entry-or-insert-with.description: Like or_insert, but the default is built by a closure only when needed.

slides.caption: The closure is not called if the key exists.

entry-and-modify.title: How Entry::and_modify works (serde_json)
entry-and-modify.description: Runs a closure on the value if the key exists.

slides.caption: Chained with or_insert for the missing case.

map-retain.title: How Map::retain works
map-retain.description: Keeps only the entries the closure approves.

slides.caption: The closure sees each key and value.
Removes without building a new map.

map-get-mut.title: How Map::get_mut works
map-get-mut.description: A mutable reference to a value by key.

slides.caption: Same as building a new Map.

map-append.title: How Map::append works
map-append.description: Moves every entry of another map into this one.

slides.caption: other is left empty; equal keys are overwritten.
Like extend, but without consuming other.

number-from-f64.title: How Number::from_f64 works
number-from-f64.description: A JSON Number from an f64; None for NaN and infinity.

slides.caption: JSON cannot represent NaN or ±∞, so they are refused.

number-as-i64.title: How Number::as_i64 works
number-as-i64.description: The number as i64 if it is a whole number that fits.

slides.caption: as_u64 / as_f64 for the other kinds.

number-as-f64.title: How Number::as_f64 works
number-as-f64.description: The number as f64 (always Some unless arbitrary precision is on).

number-is-i64.title: How Number::is_i64 works
number-is-i64.description: true if the number is stored as a signed whole number.

slides.caption: Positive integers are stored as u64 but still fit i64.

map-get-key-value.title: How Map::get_key_value works (serde_json)
map-get-key-value.description: The stored key and value for a key.

value-as-number.title: How Value::as_number works
value-as-number.description: Borrows the Number inside a JSON number.

slides.caption: Number remembers whether it is u64, i64 or f64.

value-sort-all-objects.title: How Value::sort_all_objects works
value-sort-all-objects.description: Sorts the keys of every object, at every depth.

slides.caption: Matters with the preserve_order feature; without it maps are already sorted.
